title: A low-activation structural ceramic that keeps its heat transport after fusion-relevant irradiation

concept.text: The innovation is a structural ceramic that continues to carry heat and hold its shape within useful engineering limits after irradiation representative of service in a fusion reactor. It would combine low activation—limiting the radioactivity and decay heat produced by irradiation—with high-temperature structural performance and compatibility with the selected coolant and breeder. Silicon-carbide-based materials, including SiC-fiber-reinforced SiC composites, are documented candidates for these applications.

The proposed advance concerns an integrated component, including its geometry and joints. Its thermal conductivity and dimensions could change during irradiation and still meet the goal, provided they remained inside a specified design window. Representative helium production, service loads, coolant exposure and any required leak-tightness would form part of the proposed qualification scope. Literal irradiation-invariant conductivity is a stronger condition than this concept requires.

significance.text: Fusion structures must function while exposed to irradiation and substantial thermal loads. The retained sources identify SiC-based materials as attractive because of their high-temperature capability, low activation, low decay heat and potential compatibility with relevant coolants and breeders. They describe applications in blanket and first-wall structures, flow-channel inserts and divertors. Preserving useful thermal transport and dimensional stability would address an important obstacle to making these ceramic structures credible in service.

Engineering synthesis: the revolutionary consequence would be confidence that a ceramic component could continue transferring heat and maintaining its geometry throughout a defined irradiation exposure. That confidence would require strength, coolant compatibility, joints and any necessary hermeticity to remain adequate as well. Conductivity and swelling measurements alone would not establish a qualified structural material, and success in one component design would not automatically qualify every first wall, blanket or flow-channel application.

The 2026 review connects high-temperature operation with the possibility of higher energy-conversion efficiency. A successfully qualified ceramic could therefore support more demanding thermal operating conditions, conditional on the complete component and cooling system meeting their requirements. This is an enabling materials advance; it would not by itself deliver a fusion power plant. Plasma performance, tritium systems and heat conversion would still require separate validation, and the supplied evidence does not establish the maturity of those systems.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability sought is sustained, combined performance under the conditions of a specified fusion component: useful heat transport, controlled dimensional change, adequate high-temperature strength and acceptable environmental durability. The retained review documents continuing research on degradation at high neutron damage levels, joining, deformation and irradiation-enhanced corrosion. Its discussion of bowing and tube stresses makes component shape and internal stresses part of the challenge, alongside material properties measured on small specimens.

Proposed engineering scope: the breakthrough must connect irradiation response to component operation. Changes in conductivity and dimensions must remain compatible with the chosen thermal-stress limits; joints must retain their function under relevant loads; coolant exposure must not cause unacceptable degradation; and components serving as barriers must maintain the required leak-tightness. Representative transmutation-helium production belongs in this proposed assessment, but the retained abstracts do not independently establish a particular helium requirement or hermeticity specification.

The unresolved scientific and engineering task is to demonstrate that these requirements can be satisfied together over a defined exposure and operating range. Ongoing degradation research establishes the relevance of this task, but does not prove that every possible material or component falls short. The supplied record supports a consequential qualification goal without establishing the categorical absence of the complete capability.

current_state.text: Yutai Katoh’s 2024 chapter, “SiC/SiC composites,” in Fusion Energy Technology R&D Priorities, pages 77–84, describes the material attributes motivating fusion applications and discusses remaining technical challenges. The supplied review verified the chapter’s identity and retained its abstract through the ORNL publication record. That abstract supports the application rationale and the existence of continuing development needs; it does not provide a component qualification demonstration or establish SiC’s comparative ranking among all ceramic candidates.

The supplied research cites Wantong Sun and colleagues’ 2025 Nuclear Fusion paper, “Effects of He irradiation on the microstructure and thermal conductivity of SiC,” volume 65, article 096017. It reports a conductivity decrease from approximately 190 to 4.65 W/(m·K) at 5.46 displacements per atom under room-temperature helium-ion irradiation, and attributes to the introduction a description of neutron-irradiated SiC and SiC/SiC conductivity degradation saturating after several displacements per atom. No artifact of this paper was captured for the supplied review, so its identity, numerical results, irradiation conditions and attributed passages could not be independently assessed there. These details remain explicitly unverified reports from the research input; the missing artifact is not evidence that they are false.

Even if the reported 2025 result is accurate, room-temperature helium-ion exposure of a specimen would establish behavior under those particular conditions. It would not by itself establish performance in a hot blanket neutron spectrum, with representative damage distribution, helium production, geometry, joints and service loads. The earlier general statement that SiC conductivity collapses because defects scatter phonons is also not established by the retained abstracts; this record does not support treating that mechanism or the reported numerical decrease as a universal description of service performance.

The review by Takaaki Koyanagi and colleagues, “Review of SiC material development for nuclear fusion applications,” is dated 1 August 2026 in the supplied record. Its retained abstract describes research on irradiation degradation at high neutron damage levels, deformation including bowing and tube stresses, irradiation-enhanced corrosion, joining, and opportunities for component testing under fusion-relevant conditions. The supplied evidence review verified the publication’s identity from its bibliographic metadata, including journal, article number and DOI, although the earlier research extraction had not recorded the journal title. The evidence available here remains abstract-level rather than access to the full review’s technical findings.

The retained abstracts do not establish whether a blanket component has demonstrated conductivity and dimensional stability within a specified design window throughout its intended irradiation exposure. They also do not justify the earlier categorical statement that irradiation-invariant heat transport in a blanket component has not been achieved. The supplied freshness record is empty, so the August 2026 publication cannot establish comprehensive achievement status as of 1 November 2026. The supported conclusion is that relevant development and degradation research continued in the documented literature; achievement of the complete proposed capability remains unresolved from these inputs.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: identify a particular blanket or related structural application before testing, including material architecture, geometry, service temperature, neutron spectrum, intended exposure, representative helium production, coolant or breeder environment, and mechanical loads. Select and publish the thermal-stress acceptance window and measurement methods in advance. The supplied review motivates component testing under fusion-relevant conditions, but supplies neither a particular acceptance window nor a universal qualification dose.
completion_criteria.label: Define application conditions and publish thermal-stress acceptance limits before testing

completion_criteria.text: Proposed acceptance criteria: after representative irradiation, a ceramic section would retain conductivity and dimensional stability within the selected design limits while maintaining adequate structural performance. Representative joints would avoid becoming a preferential failure path under relevant service loads. Coolant compatibility and any required hermeticity would be tested as component functions, and the low-activation objective would be assessed against the selected composition and exposure. These are proposed conditions for a convincing demonstration, not established standards supplied by the sources.
completion_criteria.label: Retain conductivity and dimensional stability within design limits after irradiation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat the measurements across independently produced specimens or component sections, report manufacturing variation and measurement uncertainty, and seek independent confirmation of the central performance results. State the demonstrated temperature, dose, helium, environment and geometry ranges, together with observed failure modes. Room-temperature ion irradiation of a coupon alone would not satisfy this combined scope. No displacement-per-atom value is proposed as a universal standard, and finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested envelope rather than universal radiation resistance.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce performance across independently produced specimens and report demonstrated limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CRM-08, “Stoichiometric silicon-carbide fiber and composites at general industrial cost,” has the closest material overlap. Affordable fibers and composites could make a successful CRM-07 component easier to manufacture and deploy, but affordability does not establish irradiation durability, and irradiation durability does not establish general industrial cost. The two entries address distinct barriers.

Roster-based synthesis: CRM-01, room-temperature tensile ductility in bulk polycrystalline structural ceramics, concerns mechanical deformation and damage tolerance; CRM-05, repeated in-service restoration of strength after critical cracks, concerns repair. Either could complement structural reliability, but neither demonstrates retained thermal transport under irradiation. CRM-02, long service in air above the silica limit, overlaps in high-temperature structural endurance while addressing an oxidizing-air environment rather than the neutron, coolant and breeder conditions central to CRM-07.

Roster-based synthesis: CRM-04, densification without a high-temperature furnace cycle, and CRM-11, net-shape additive manufacturing of fully dense technical ceramics, address manufacturing routes that could assist component production. Their success would not establish irradiation performance, joint durability or environmental compatibility. CRM-12, large transparent ceramics approaching theoretical failure strength, overlaps in controlling defects and structural reliability, but its optical function and strength objective remain distinct from retained heat transport in fusion service.

Roster-based synthesis: CRM-03, a practical lithium-metal solid-state ceramic electrolyte; CRM-06, a useful ambient-pressure, room-temperature superconducting ceramic conductor; CRM-09, ceramic membranes replacing cryogenic olefin–paraffin distillation; and CRM-10, an earth-abundant oxide converting sunlight and water into fuel, all seek useful ceramic functions under demanding operating conditions. Their central goals concern ionic transport, superconductivity, molecular separation and solar-fuel conversion, respectively. Success in any of them would not establish the structural and irradiation capability sought by CRM-07, and each remains a separate innovation.

unresolved_issues: The Sun et al. paper lacks a captured artifact, leaving its bibliographic identity, reported conductivity values, dose, conditions and attributed saturation discussion unverified within the supplied review.
No bounded freshness assessment establishes the complete capability’s achievement status as of 1 November 2026.
No particular component design, published thermal-stress window, intended exposure or acceptable conductivity and dimensional-change limits is supplied.
The design-specific helium-production requirement, hermeticity requirement and methods for validating them remain unspecified.
The retained abstracts do not establish comparative leadership among ceramic candidates or substantiate the generalized phonon-scattering explanation.
Full chapter and review findings are unavailable in the supplied evidence, limiting assessment of demonstrated performance, joint behavior, corrosion and component qualification.

brief.title: Ceramic reactor parts that keep carrying heat
possible: Fusion reactor designers could use ceramic parts that keep moving heat and holding their shape after radiation exposure like that expected in service. The parts would also limit the radioactivity and heat that radiation creates in the material.
why: Fusion reactor structures face radiation and intense heat together. A ceramic that withstands both could give engineers confidence that parts will keep working throughout a defined operating life.
Operating at higher temperatures could help future fusion plants turn heat into electricity more efficiently.

sources.cited_for: It supports testing how radiation changes the material’s ability to carry heat.

shown: Researchers have studied fibre-reinforced silicon carbide in shapes relevant to reactor parts. Koyanagi and colleagues describe work on channels bending under uneven radiation, stresses in tubes with uneven temperatures, and corrosion worsened by radiation.
missing: A complete part still needs to demonstrate useful heat transport, stable shape and adequate strength together under representative conditions.
Joints must retain their function under load, cooling fluids must cause acceptable damage, and any required barriers must stay leak-tight.
The chosen material must meet its limits on radiation-induced radioactivity and heat over the intended exposure.

milestones.explanation: Separately made samples would reproduce the results, with independent confirmation, manufacturing variation, uncertainty and failure limits reported. This would establish how broadly the demonstrated performance applies.

page.title: Irradiation-qualified SiC/SiC fusion blanket structures
page.definition: SiC/SiC—silicon carbide fibres reinforcing a silicon carbide matrix—forms a load-bearing fusion blanket component that retains its specified heat transport, dimensions and strength throughout its irradiation lifetime. Its composition meets the component's limits on irradiation-induced radioactivity and decay heat.

goal.need: SiC/SiC blanket design recommendations adopted a conductivity of 20 W/(m·K) and a 600–1000 °C operating window. A 2015 fission-reactor experiment found mechanical degradation above 70 displacements per atom, a measure of lattice damage, at 573–1073 K, with no evidence of progressive swelling or thermal-conductivity evolution. Retained heat transport alone therefore does not establish structural lifetime.

statements.quote: It is clear that consistent design codes and standards need to be formulated for ceramics operating at high temperature and under irradiation.
Require qualified materials for blanket and first wall structural components.
statements.context: Core Challenge A2 of the Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap; the roadmap includes SiC and SiC-SiC among candidate structural materials.

statements.quote: In all cases, the low activation of SiC reduces the burden of waste management

completion.title: A SiC/SiC blanket component meets its design limits throughout its specified fusion irradiation lifetime.
completion.criterion: An integrated SiC/SiC blanket component, including joints, meets the selected design's published limits on thermal conductivity, dimensional change, strength, coolant/breeder compatibility and any required leak-tightness throughout its specified irradiation lifetime. Testing reproduces the design's temperature, neutron spectrum, dose, helium/hydrogen production and thermal/mechanical loads. Its composition also meets specified induced-activity and decay-heat limits. The exposure and acceptance values are application-specific; no universal dose or retained-conductivity percentage is assigned.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas synthesis of component qualification goals; no outside body located specifies this combined acceptance test.
completion.basis: The search covered the SiC/SiC Town Meeting recommendations, DOE's 2026 fusion roadmap, the NEA nuclear-material readiness scale and published ASME/RCC qualification pathways. No single test combining conductivity, dimensional stability, activation and service exposure was found. The component-specific lifetime demonstration follows the published qualification principle of intended function, environment and lifetime; construction-code compliance alone does not prescribe every fusion environmental effect.

milestones.title: SiC/SiC demonstrates its material concept in laboratory experiments, reaching nuclear-material TRL 3.
milestones.criterion: Technology readiness level (TRL) 3 requires laboratory verification and characterization of mechanical, environmental and preliminary irradiation behaviour. Laboratory evidence includes the 2000 meeting's report of unirradiated MER composites conducting 35 W/(m·K) transversely at 1000 °C.
milestones.set_by: OECD Nuclear Energy Agency Expert Group on Innovative Structural Materials, 2021, Table 1, TRL 3. The criterion appears only in a table and applies generally to nuclear structural materials.

milestones.title: SiC/SiC completes test-reactor irradiation under relevant conditions, reaching nuclear-material TRL 4.
milestones.criterion: TRL 4 requires experiments under relevant reactor conditions, including test-reactor irradiation that may be incompletely representative. The 2015 HFIR study tested Hi-Nicalon Type S composites above 70 dpa at 573–1073 K: swelling and conductivity showed no progressive evolution, while mechanical properties degraded.
milestones.set_by: OECD Nuclear Energy Agency Expert Group on Innovative Structural Materials, 2021, Table 1, TRL 4. The criterion appears only in a table and applies generally to nuclear structural materials.

milestones.title: SiC/SiC behaviour is established through single- and multiple-effects tests, reaching nuclear-material TRL 5.
milestones.criterion: TRL 5 requires single- and multiple-effects tests establishing performance for a representative reactor system, with bench-scale fabrication/joining. Relevant research described in the 2026 review includes channel bowing under neutron-flux gradients, tube stresses under temperature gradients and irradiation-enhanced corrosion. These results concern particular effects and geometries.
milestones.set_by: OECD Nuclear Energy Agency Expert Group on Innovative Structural Materials, 2021, Table 1, TRL 5. The criterion appears only in a table and applies generally to nuclear structural materials.

milestones.title: A SiC/SiC blanket prototype is tested under relevant irradiation conditions, reaching TRL 6.
milestones.criterion: TRL 6 requires a representative prototype, relevant irradiation/property testing, material behaviour laws and full-scale prototype fabrication/joining. General Atomics reported manufacturing components up to 12 ft long in 2026; component size alone does not establish this integrated demonstration.
milestones.set_by: OECD Nuclear Energy Agency Expert Group on Innovative Structural Materials, 2021, Table 1, TRL 6. The criterion appears only in a table and applies generally to nuclear structural materials.

milestones.title: A SiC/SiC blanket prototype demonstrates operation under reactor conditions, reaching TRL 7.
milestones.criterion: TRL 7 requires prototype demonstration in operational conditions. For this entry, the prototype is a SiC/SiC fusion blanket component; initial operation precedes demonstration over its complete specified irradiation lifetime.
milestones.set_by: OECD Nuclear Energy Agency Expert Group on Innovative Structural Materials, 2021, Table 1, TRL 7. The criterion appears only in a table and applies generally to nuclear structural materials.
